Fluid losses: Enquire about severe diarrhoea, vomiting, overt gastrointestinal bleeding (haematemesis, melaena), or reduced intake in hot weather.
Bleeding (most common acute complication): presents as haematemesis or melena; mortality rises if not controlled promptly.

qs.q: A 50-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis presents with severe haematemesis. Emergency endoscopy reveals bleeding oesophageal varices. Which anatomical vascular communication serves as the primary inflow pathway driving these dilated submucosal varices?
o: Splenic vein to superior mesenteric link
Inferior vena cava to renal vein pathway
Portal vein to azygos system communication
Internal jugular to subclavian junction
Common iliac to internal iliac channel
qs.e: Oesophageal varices form via portosystemic collateral channels connecting the portal system (via left gastric vein) with the systemic circulation (via azygos/hemiazygos veins).

qs.q: A 52-year-old man presents with massive haematemesis, confusion, and a systolic blood pressure of 85 mmHg. Which initial management step is the highest priority?
o: Emergency upper gastrointestinal endoscopy within 2 hours
Urgent administration of intravenous proton pump inhibitor
Immediate tracheal intubation for airway protection
Insertion of a nasogastric tube for gastric lavage
qs.e: Airway protection via early intubation is the priority for massive haematemesis or altered consciousness due to aspiration risk. Endoscopy and drug therapy follow after resuscitation has been initiated.

qs.q: A 54-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis presents with massive haematemesis. While awaiting urgent endoscopy, which vasoactive agent is the most appropriate initial pharmacological intervention to reduce portal pressure?
o: Single IV bolus of somatostatin only
Continuous IV infusion of vasopressin alone
IV bolus of terlipressin then continuous infusion
Continuous IV dopamine titrated to urine output
qs.e: Terlipressin is a first-line vasoactive agent for acute variceal bleeding that does not require concurrent nitroglycerin. Vasopressin is less favored as monotherapy due to the high risk of coronary ischaemia, which necessitates co-administration of nitroglycerin.

qs.q: A patient presents with massive haematemesis after prolonged episodes of retching following acute alcohol intoxication. Endoscopy reveals a linear mucosal tear crossing the gastroesophageal junction. What is the most appropriate management approach?
o: Emergency surgical repair and oversewing
Endoscopic variceal band ligation
Immediate transjugular portosystemic shunt
Conservative management and observation
qs.e: Mallory-Weiss tears are superficial mucosal lacerations associated with vomiting that heal rapidly and completely without surgery. Boerhaave syndrome involves transmural tears requiring emergency surgery.

qs.q: A 45-year-old male presents with acute epigastric pain and haematemesis following heavy alcohol and NSAID use. Which histological feature is expected on biopsy?
o: Dominant plasma cells and chronic lymphocytes
Heavy surface epithelial infiltration by eosinophils
Replacement of parietal cells by mucus cells
Mucosal infiltration with neutrophils and oedema
qs.e: Acute gastritis is characterized histologically by mucosal infiltration with neutrophils and oedema, often presenting as erosive and haemorrhagic. Plasma cells and lymphocytes are characteristic of chronic gastritis instead.

qs.q: A patient with advanced alcoholic cirrhosis develops sudden massive haematemesis. Emergency endoscopy reveals ruptured oesophageal varices. What is the mortality rate from this first bleeding episode?
o: Approximately fifty percent despite medical intervention
Approximately ten to fifteen percent even without treatment
Approximately twenty-five to thirty percent with management
Approximately seventy to eighty percent without ligation
qs.e: Approximately 50% of patients die from the first variceal bleeding episode from direct haemorrhage or hepatic coma from the protein load combined with hypovolaemic shock.

qs.q: A 42-year-old male presents after a binge drinking episode with haematemesis. Endoscopy shows linear tears crossing the gastroesophageal junction without perforation into the mediastinum. What distinguishes this from Boerhaave syndrome?
o: Mallory-Weiss requires surgical repair while Boerhaave heals spontaneously
Mallory-Weiss tears occur in the stomach while Boerhaave occurs in the oesophagus
Mallory-Weiss tears are caused by alcohol while Boerhaave is caused by vomiting
Mallory-Weiss tears are superficial while Boerhaave involves transmural perforation
qs.e: Mallory-Weiss tears are superficial mucosal lacerations that heal spontaneously. Boerhaave syndrome involves transmural perforation leading to mediastinitis — a life-threatening surgical emergency.

ai.title: Haematemesis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding presenting as vomiting of blood. In low‑resource settings the most common causes are peptic ulcer disease and variceal bleed from chronic liver disease. Rapid assessment, resuscitation and cause‑directed therapy are essential.

sections.p: Haematemesis is the expectoration of blood originating proximal to the ligament of Treitz. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by bedside observation of colour and consistency of the vomitus.
b: Bright red = fresh arterial bleed
Coffee‑ground = older blood mixed with gastric acid

sections.p: Severity is graded by haemodynamic impact and volume loss. The Rockall score (age, shock, comorbidity, diagnosis, stigmata) predicts mortality; in low‑resource settings use simple shock criteria.
b: Moderate: orthostatic drop ≥20 mmHg or HR >100 bpm

sections.p: Categorise by source and epidemiology. In East Africa the top three are:
b: Peptic ulcer disease (H. pylori, NSAIDs, alcohol)
Portal hypertension with oesophageal/gastric varices (cirrhosis, schistosomiasis, hepatitis B/C)
Mucosal erosions from severe malaria or typhoid

sections.p: Patients often appear pale, clammy and may have orthostatic hypotension. Associated features point to the aetiology.
b: History of chronic liver disease → varices
Recent NSAID use or dyspepsia → ulcer
Fever, diarrhoea → infectious ulceration

sections.p: When endoscopy is unavailable, manage as variceal bleed if stigmata of chronic liver disease are present; otherwise treat as ulcer bleed.

t.b: Is the patient anaemic? A drop >2 g/dL suggests significant loss.
Is there shock? Systolic <90 mmHg or a fall ≥20 mmHg on standing indicates severe bleed.

t.a: Nasogastric aspirate (if tube can be placed)
t.b: Is there ongoing bleed? Fresh blood confirms active upper GI source.
Is immunosuppression present? HIV raises risk of varices and ulcer disease.
Is there portal hypertension? Dilated portal vein, splenomegaly support variceal source.
What is the exact lesion? Allows therapeutic banding or injection.

sections.p: Uncontrolled bleeding can lead to hypovolemic shock, aspiration pneumonia, and multi‑organ failure.
b: Persistent vomiting of fresh blood >30 min
Mental status change
Refractory hypotension despite fluids

sections.p: Resuscitate first, then target the cause.
b: IV crystalloid 20 mL/kg bolus; give blood if Hb <7 g/dL or ongoing shock
Proton‑pump inhibitor IV (e.g., omeprazole) for suspected ulcer bleed
Octreotide infusion for suspected variceal bleed (reduces portal pressure)
Antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone) for cirrhotics to prevent infection
If endoscopy available, band varices or inject epinephrine/thermal therapy for ulcers

sections.p: After stabilisation arrange definitive therapy and secondary prevention.
b: Eradicate H. pylori if ulcer confirmed
Non‑selective beta‑blocker (e.g., propranolol) for variceal prophylaxis
Vaccinate against hepatitis B, counsel on alcohol reduction
Educate on NSAID avoidance and use of gastro‑protective agents
Hemoptysis – blood coughed up, usually frothy, associated with respiratory signs
Post‑nasal drip of blood – originates from epistaxis, not GI tract
Mouth or dental bleeding – localized oral source
Normal haemoglobin early in bleed – dilutional effect may mask loss
Beta‑blocker use masking tachycardia – assess orthostatic change instead
Negative nasogastric aspirate does not exclude bleed if tube placement failed

whenToSeekHelp: Systolic BP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg despite fluids

faq.q: Why is coffee‑ground vomitus less urgent than bright red blood?
faq.a: It indicates slower, older bleeding that is often self‑limited, whereas bright red suggests an active arterial source.

faq.q: Can a patient on beta‑blockers be assumed stable if pulse is normal?
faq.a: No; beta‑blockers blunt tachycardia, so assess blood pressure and orthostatic response.
When the source is unclear, bleeding persists after resuscitation, or therapeutic intervention (banding, clipping) is needed.

exam: What immediate steps do you take for a patient with haematemesis and orthostatic hypotension? — Assess airway, give two large‑bore IVs, start fluid resuscitation, obtain bedside haemoglobin and consider blood transfusion.

How would you differentiate variceal bleed from peptic ulcer bleed at the bedside? — Look for stigmata of chronic liver disease, history of alcohol or hepatitis, and consider ultrasound for portal hypertension; ulcer bleed is more likely with NSAID use and epigastric pain.
Why is octreotide preferred over vasopressin in suspected variceal bleeding? — Octreotide has fewer cardiac side‑effects and does not require intensive monitoring.

A patient on bisoprolol presents with haematemesis but a pulse of 80 bpm. How do you interpret the vital signs? — The beta‑blocker masks tachycardia; rely on blood pressure and orthostatic change to gauge shock.
If endoscopy is unavailable, what pharmacologic regimen covers both ulcer and variceal sources? — Give IV proton‑pump inhibitor plus octreotide infusion; add antibiotics if cirrhosis is present.
What are the indications for blood transfusion in acute upper GI bleed? — Hb <7 g/dL, or <9 g/dL with cardiovascular disease or ongoing massive bleed.
Explain why prophylactic antibiotics are given to cirrhotic patients with haematemesis. — They reduce the risk of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and improve survival.
What long‑term measure prevents recurrent variceal bleed? — Non‑selective beta‑blocker therapy or endoscopic variceal ligation.
